title: Internationally trained doctors and nurses: your first year of money in Canada
seoTitle: Trained abroad: your first year of money in Canada
description: Licensing takes time and your income may start late. How tax, credit, savings and benefits work in a first year while your credentials are being recognized.
question: How should I plan my money in Canada while my licence and credentials are still being recognized?
figuresAsOf: 2026 TFSA limit and CRA and FCAC guidance as published on the pages listed under Sources
problem: A physician or nurse trained abroad often arrives with years of experience and no Canadian licence yet. The risk is not a lack of skill. It is a gap between the day your costs start and the day your professional income does, and nobody can tell you exactly how long that gap will be.
overview: Plan around the gap, not the salary. Your regulator sets the steps, fees and order for licensing in your province, and the timeline can change. A sensible first-year plan asks how many months your savings can cover if recognition takes longer than hoped.

Tax residency starts early. CRA says you become a resident for income tax purposes when you have enough residential ties in Canada, and that for most newcomers this starts the first day you live here. Your first return is due after the year you arrive. CRA’s own example: someone who arrived in 2025 files that return by April 30, 2026. The deadline is June 15 if you or your spouse or common-law partner are self-employed. CRA also uses your return to work out benefits and credits, even if you have no income to report, and says you can apply for benefits and credits as soon as you arrive if you meet the eligibility criteria.

Savings you bring with you. A Canadian resident who holds specified foreign property with a total cost of more than CAD $100,000 at any time in the year files Form T1135 with their tax return. The test uses cost, not market value. You do not file it for the year you first become a resident. In later years, the cost of property you owned on arrival is its fair market value on the day you became a resident. The rules are technical, so a tax professional is the right person to confirm what applies to you.

Registered accounts start from zero. TFSA room begins on the day you become a resident, if you are 18 or older, and nothing accumulates for the years before. The 2026 limit is $7,000. RRSP room is generally built from 18% of your earned income in the previous year, up to the annual maximum, so it can be small in your first year. An FHSA requires you to be a resident, 18 or older, and a first-time home buyer as CRA defines it, and you give the issuer your Social Insurance Number.

Credit starts here too. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC) says Canadian credit scores usually range from 300 to 900 and come from reports kept by two main bureaus, Equifax and TransUnion. It notes that a limited credit history may make it harder to borrow, get a credit card or rent a home. Do not assume your history from home carries over; ask each lender what it will consider.

Banking and your SIN. Banks must confirm your identity with original identification, and foreign passports are on the approved list. Some institutions may ask you to visit a branch in person. A Social Insurance Number is a nine-digit number needed to work in Canada or access government programs and benefits. A temporary resident’s SIN starts with 9 and expires with their immigration documents. It is private, and you are responsible for protecting it.

Help with licensing costs. The federal Foreign Credential Recognition program lists loans of up to $30,000, offered through participating organizations, to help with licensing and exam fees, additional training or tuition. Eligibility depends on your immigration status and province. A loan is still debt, so the terms matter as much as the amount.

Sending money home. FCAC says the real cost of sending money abroad includes transfer fees, exchange-rate costs and charges paid by the recipient, and that a low fee may be offset by a less favourable exchange rate. Compare the total, not just the headline fee.

example.title: How long recognition takes changes the whole plan
example.intro: Hypothetical figures. A household arrives with CAD $30,000 in savings. Monthly living costs are $3,200, and exam, licensing and preparation costs are $6,000 in total. The table ignores any interim income to show the effect of timing alone.
notes: All numbers here are invented to show how the arithmetic works. They are not typical costs and not a prediction of how long recognition takes.
Six more months of waiting turns a small shortfall into a large one. That is why the longer timeline, not the hopeful one, is the useful number to plan around.
Interim income, a partner’s earnings, family support or a loan would change the picture. Each has its own trade-offs.

misunderstandings.myth: My credit history and my credentials come with me.
misunderstandings.reality: Credit generally starts from the beginning here, and professional licensing is a separate process run for your profession in your province or territory. The federal program describes recognition as verifying that foreign education, skills and experience are equivalent to Canadian standards.

misunderstandings.myth: If I have no Canadian income yet, I do not need to think about a tax return.
misunderstandings.reality: CRA says it uses your return each year, even if you have no income to report, and that it works out benefits and credits from it. Your first return is due after the year you arrive.

misunderstandings.myth: Money I keep abroad is not CRA’s concern once I live here.
misunderstandings.reality: A Canadian resident whose specified foreign property cost more than CAD $100,000 at any time in a year generally files Form T1135 with that year’s return, except for the year they first become a resident. Ask a tax professional what applies to you.

misunderstandings.myth: I will have as much TFSA and RRSP room as colleagues who have lived here for years.
misunderstandings.reality: TFSA room starts on the day you become a resident, and RRSP room builds from earned income. Newcomers usually start with much less.

misunderstandings.myth: A low transfer fee means sending money home is cheap.
misunderstandings.reality: FCAC warns that providers may make up for a low fee with a less favourable exchange rate. Compare the total cost, including what the recipient pays.

tradeoffs: Money you commit to a registered account or send abroad is money not available for licensing fees and living costs while your income is uncertain. Think about how quickly you could reach it.
A credit card builds a Canadian record if you use it responsibly, but carries high interest if the balance is not paid in full.
A recognition loan can cover exam and training fees, but it adds a repayment you will carry before your professional income starts.
Taking interim work can protect your savings, but it may take time from exam preparation. The right balance differs for each person.
Rules differ by profession, province, immigration status and family situation. Treat this guide as a starting point and check with your regulator and the official sources below.
questions: What are all the licensing steps, fees and realistic timelines for my profession in my province, according to the regulator?
